content: Overactive bladder (OAB) is a clinical condition characterized by distressing urinary symptoms, including urgency, increased frequency of urination, and nocturia (waking up at night to urinate). If urinary incontinence is present, the condition is referred to as OAB-wet, whereas the absence of incontinence is termed OAB-dry. OAB significantly impacts the quality of life of affected individuals. The International Continence Society defines OAB as the presence of urinary urgency, typically accompanied by frequency and nocturia, with or without urgency urinary incontinence, in the absence of urinary tract infection or other identifiable pathology. OAB is often associated with conditions such as neurological injuries or diseases, urinary tract infections, bladder inflammation, and bladder outlet obstruction. The symptoms of OAB are caused by spontaneous contractions of the detrusor muscle, which increase intravesical pressure during bladder filling. These contractions may result from abnormalities in the nerves, smooth muscle, or urothelium of the bladder. Among the various urinary symptoms, urgency is considered the primary symptom and is the key parameter for diagnosing and monitoring treatment response in OAB patients. The global prevalence of OAB is estimated to range between 12% and 17%, with the condition becoming more common with advancing age. OAB is particularly prevalent in individuals over 40 years of age, affecting both men and women. In the United States, the National Overactive Bladder Evaluation (NOBLE) program reported a prevalence of 16.9% in women and 16% in men. Similarly, in Europe, the overall prevalence is 16.6%, with comparable rates between genders. Studies have shown that storage symptoms, such as urgency, frequency, and nocturia, are more frequently reported in women than in men. Behavioral therapy is the first-line treatment for OAB. This includes patient education on bladder training, bladder control strategies, pelvic floor muscle training, and fluid management. When pharmacologic treatment is required, antimuscarinic drugs are the current first-line option. These include medications such as darifenacin, fesoterodine, oxybutynin, solifenacin, tolterodine, trospium, and propiverine. These drugs work by antagonizing cholinergic muscarinic receptors, thereby inhibiting parasympathetic impulses and reducing detrusor muscle contractions. However, antimuscarinic agents are associated with side effects such as dry mouth and constipation. Other treatment options for OAB include intermittent catheterization, sacral neuromodulation, and posterior tibial nerve stimulation. Onabotulinumtoxin A has also been approved for patients who do not respond adequately to anticholinergic therapy. Cochrane systematic reviews have evaluated many of these treatment options, including anticholinergics, pelvic floor muscle training, bladder training, intermittent catheterization, sacral neuromodulation, and onabotulinumtoxin A. In June 2012, the United States Food and Drug Administration (FDA) approved a new class of drugs, beta-3 adrenergic receptor agonists, for the treatment of OAB. This drug class includes agents such as mirabegron, ritobegron, and solabegron. These medications work by activating beta-3 adrenergic receptors, which relax the detrusor muscle during the bladder's storage phase, thereby increasing bladder capacity. By inhibiting bladder afferent nerves, these drugs improve the symptom of urgency, which is the hallmark symptom of OAB. Beta-adrenergic receptors are classified into three subtypes: beta-1, beta-2, and beta-3. Studies on cellular and messenger RNA expression have shown that the majority of beta-adrenergic receptors in the human detrusor muscle are of the beta-3 subtype. Activation of these receptors promotes detrusor relaxation and enhances urine storage, making them a promising therapeutic target for OAB, particularly in patients with storage symptoms. Randomized controlled trials have demonstrated that beta-3 adrenergic receptor agonists significantly reduce OAB symptoms in patients with moderate to severe symptoms over treatment periods of at least eight weeks. These drugs have shown dose-dependent improvements in reducing the number of micturition episodes, with good safety and tolerability profiles. Additionally, beta-3 adrenergic receptor agonists have been shown to effectively control OAB symptoms, such as frequency and incontinence, with fewer side effects like dry mouth and constipation compared to antimuscarinic drugs or placebo. However, some adverse effects have been reported with certain beta-3 adrenergic receptor agonists, including hypertension, nasopharyngitis, urinary tract infections, and headaches. Despite their promising potential, the efficacy of beta-3 adrenergic receptor agonists has shown only small differences when compared to anticholinergics and other treatment options. Furthermore, inconsistencies in the adverse events associated with these drugs have been noted in clinical trials. A meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials involving beta-3 adrenergic receptor agonists could provide a clearer understanding of their efficacy and tolerability profiles, particularly in comparison to other treatment options. Such an analysis would help clinicians make more informed decisions regarding the utility of these drugs in the management of OAB.
